title: Adaptive Variable Resolution 2.5D Lidar Mapping for Dynamic Environment Perception
description:
• Background:
Autonomous navigation depends on the ability of a vehicle to perceive its surroundings with high precision. While 3D Lidar point clouds provide rich spatial data, processing millions of points in real-time creates immense computational bottlenecks and memory latency. Conversely, standard 2D occupancy grids lose critical height information necessary for detecting curbs, potholes, or overhanging obstacles. To balance precision and performance, there is a need for a 'foveated' mapping approach-similar to human vision- where the immediate vicinity is rendered in high detail for safety, and distant areas are simplified to reduce the processing load.
• Description:
The goal is to build a deep learning pipeline that transforms raw Lidar point clouds into a variable resolution 2.5D grid (an elevation map with semantic layers). The system must perform three primary tasks:
1. Terrain Analysis: Distinguish between drivable surfaces and non-drivable terrain.
2. Object Detection: Identify and classify static obstacles (walls, poles) and dynamic objects (pedestrians, other vehicles).
3. Adaptive Spatial Representation: Implement a non-uniform grid where the cell size increases as the distance from the sensor increases. This requires a sophisticated data structure that can handle variable resolution without causing alignment errors or data loss during the projection from 3D to 2.5D.
• Expected Solution:
A software framework consisting of:
• A Deep Learning Model: A network (e.g., PointNet++ or a Sparse Convolutional Neural Network) capable of semantic segmentation of point clouds into terrain, static obstacles, and moving objects.
• Variable Resolution Grid Engine: An algorithm that projects classified 3D points into a 2.5D grid where the resolution is high (e.g., 5cm cells)
within a 10m radius and decreases (e.g., 50cm cells) up to a 100m radius.
• Real-time Visualization: A dashboard showing the 2.5D map with distinct color-coding for terrain and objects, demonstrating a significant reduction in memory usage compared to a uniform high-resolution 3D map.
• Performance Metrics: Evidence of low latency (high FPS) and high accuracy in object classification across varying distances.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on deep learning, autonomous, neural applied to a transportation & logistics problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Transportation & Logistics. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on sensor, model, real-time. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 21/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: Adaptive Variable Resolution 2.5D Lidar Mapping for Dynamic Environment Perception

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that processes raw LiDAR data the way human vision works, sharp detail right in front of you, less detail farther away, so an autonomous vehicle can perceive its surroundings in real time without drowning in millions of data points.
overview.why_it_matters: Full 3D LiDAR processing is too computationally heavy for real-time use, but flat 2D maps lose critical safety information like curbs and potholes. This 'foveated' approach solves both problems at once.
pain_points: Full 3D LiDAR point cloud processing creates real-time computational bottlenecks.
Standard 2D occupancy grids lose critical height information for hazard detection.
No efficient middle-ground representation balances precision and performance.
overview.background: Autonomous navigation needs precise environment perception, but 3D LiDAR is computationally heavy for real-time use while 2D grids lose important height-based safety information, motivating a variable-resolution 2.5D approach.
overview.whats_being_asked: A deep learning pipeline transforming raw LiDAR point clouds into a variable-resolution 2.5D elevation grid with semantic layers, performing terrain analysis, object detection, and adaptive (foveated) spatial representation.
expected_solution: Static and dynamic object detection and classification.
Non-uniform grid with cell size increasing by distance from sensor.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. The 'foveated' variable-resolution approach to LiDAR processing is a genuinely clever, non-obvious solution to a real computational bottleneck, real technical creativity beyond standard perception pipelines.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires point cloud processing, terrain/object classification, and a genuinely novel adaptive data structure implementation together, real technical depth.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine robotics/perception/deep learning expertise, similar to SIH26037, a narrower, more technical field.

innovation.note: The foveated, variable-resolution approach is a genuinely clever technical solution, not a standard perception pipeline.

invention.note: Combines point cloud processing, classification, and a novel adaptive data structure, substantial technical breadth.

technical_feasibility.note: Public LiDAR datasets exist for autonomous driving research, reducing data-sourcing risk relative to many other PS in this batch.

impact_and_benefits.note: A foundational perception-layer improvement with broad applicability to autonomous systems generally.

architecture.note: Point cloud input, classification models, and the adaptive grid data structure need to work together, but within a well-contained software pipeline.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with robotics/perception ML experience. Public datasets exist, reducing data risk, and the core technical challenge (implementing the adaptive resolution structure correctly) is well-scoped and demoable.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Public LiDAR datasets for autonomous driving research are genuinely available, a real data-sourcing advantage relative to many other PS in this batch.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: The adaptive, non-uniform grid data structure itself is the genuinely hard, differentiating part, teams that build standard terrain/object classification without the actual foveated adaptive structure would miss the PS's core ask.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm your team can implement the actual variable-resolution adaptive grid structure (not just standard classification on a uniform grid), that's the specific technical differentiator this PS is testing for.

idea_0_4: Source a public LiDAR point cloud dataset for autonomous driving (several established research datasets exist).
Design your adaptive grid data structure explicitly, this is the core technical challenge, plan it before building classification models.
Split: one person on terrain/object classification, one on the adaptive data structure implementation.
prototype_4_22: Build terrain classification (drivable vs. non-drivable) on your sample point cloud data.
Build object detection/classification for static and dynamic objects.
Start implementing the actual variable-resolution grid structure, cell size increasing with distance.
integration_22_30: Connect classification outputs into your adaptive grid representation.
Test and measure the actual computational efficiency gain versus a standard uniform-resolution grid, this comparison is your key evidence.
Test on a genuinely dynamic scenario (moving pedestrian/vehicle in the scene) to confirm the pipeline handles dynamic objects correctly.
polish_30_36: Build a clear visualization showing your foveated grid, high detail near the sensor, reduced detail farther away.
Rehearse explaining the specific computational efficiency gain your adaptive structure achieves versus standard approaches.
Prepare to discuss real-time performance implications for actual autonomous vehicle deployment.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show a live visualization of your adaptive grid alongside a standard uniform-resolution grid processing the same data, and the measured computational time difference, that direct comparison proves the actual value of your foveated approach.

strengths: Public datasets genuinely available, reducing data-sourcing risk.
Technically creative, differentiated approach (foveated mapping) rather than a standard perception pipeline.
weaknesses: Requires genuine robotics/perception ML expertise, not broadly accessible to a general team.
The adaptive grid structure itself (the actual differentiator) is real, non-trivial engineering, easy to under-build and end up with just standard classification.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Robotics/perception-heavy, with a dedicated person on the adaptive data structure specifically, don't let it become an afterthought.
team_fit.approach: Prototype the adaptive grid data structure early, even with placeholder classification data, this de-risks the most technically novel part of the build.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard point cloud classification models using existing architectures and libraries.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing the actual variable-resolution adaptive grid data structure correctly, that's a genuine algorithms/data-structures engineering challenge requiring real design thought, not a default pattern.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: AI-scaffolded standard classification without the genuine adaptive resolution structure would deliver a conventional perception pipeline, missing the PS's specific, differentiating technical ask.

data_resource_availability.status: Public LiDAR point cloud datasets for autonomous driving research are genuinely available and usable for a credible demo.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Not needed, real data access is not a significant constraint here.

judge_qna.question: What's the actual computational efficiency gain from your adaptive grid versus a standard uniform-resolution approach?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Present your measured processing time comparison directly, real numbers on the same dataset, that quantified gain is the core proof of your foveated approach's value.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the accuracy tradeoff, if any, from reduced resolution at distance?

judge_qna.question: How does your system handle a fast-moving object that starts far away (low resolution) and approaches quickly?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe how your adaptive structure updates as objects move between resolution zones, and whether there's any detection lag or discontinuity at the zone boundary, this is a genuine edge case worth addressing directly.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your system's behavior if an object is detected right at a resolution-zone boundary?
